answers.answer: With one judgement per item there is no second reading to compare against, so an agreement figure cannot be computed at all, and nothing in the file records how confident the labeller was or whether anyone else would have decided the same way. DocLayNet paid for the second and third reading deliberately: 7059 pages carry two instances of human annotation and 1591 carry three, bringing the corpus to 91104 annotation instances. The authors list the redundancy as a contribution in its own right, since it is what makes annotation uncertainty and quality control analysis possible, and the dataset card describes it as allowing an upper bound on achievable prediction accuracy to be estimated.
accept: says an agreement number cannot be computed at all when each item is labelled once
names the redundant subset, thousands of pages annotated twice and a smaller set three times
says the redundancy buys an estimate of annotation uncertainty
says it buys an upper bound on achievable prediction accuracy

answers.answer: Hold one person's boxes as though they were a model's prediction, hold a second person's boxes as though they were the ground truth, and run the same scoring function the models go through. DocLayNet computes the inter-annotator agreement as the mAP at 0.5 to 0.95 metric between pairwise annotations from the triple-annotated pages. Three annotations on one page supply more than one such pair, and the pairs do not all score the same, which is why the result is an accuracy range rather than one number.
accept: treats one annotator's labels as the prediction and another's as the ground truth
runs the model's own metric over that pair, mAP at 0.5 to 0.95 in DocLayNet
says the comparison is pairwise across the triple-annotated pages
explains that several pairs per page produce a range rather than a single value

answers.answer: You cannot subtract one from the other, so you cannot state a gap, and a ceiling that cannot be compared with a model score is a ceiling you cannot use. DocLayNet avoids that by computing agreement with the same metric the detectors are scored with, mAP at 0.5 to 0.95 between pairwise annotations on triple-annotated pages. Section 5 then does the subtraction directly, reporting that the variation between models is low but that all of them sit between 6 and 10% below the mAP computed from the pairwise human annotations.
accept: says the two cannot be subtracted or compared, so no gap can be computed
concludes that a ceiling in a different unit is unusable as a target
says DocLayNet measures agreement with the same metric used to score models
notes that section 5 subtracts the two directly to report the human to model gap

answers.answer: Quote the range, 6 to 10%. The results section is where the measurement is actually reported and the abstract is a compression of it, taking the top of the range as a single approximate figure. Neither statement is wrong, so the right move is not to average them or to pick one quietly: note the discrepancy. The habit generalises past this paper, and where an abstract and a results section disagree about a number, the results section is the one to carry into your own writing.
accept: picks the 6 to 10% range from section 5
reasons that the results section reports the measurement while the abstract compresses it
says the discrepancy is stated rather than averaged away or resolved silently
generalises the rule to any abstract that disagrees with its own results section

answers.answer: Neither annotator made a mistake, and this is DocLayNet's own example: with subfigures, one annotator draws a single figure bounding box while another annotates each subfigure separately. Documents with complex layouts have different but equally acceptable interpretations. An evaluation admitting one correct answer per item scores one reading wrong regardless, so the penalty is a property of the evaluation rather than of the system being evaluated. Measuring agreement makes that cost visible as the distance between the ceiling and a perfect score, instead of leaving it buried inside every model's error.
accept: says both readings are defensible and neither annotator erred
says complex layouts admit different but equally acceptable interpretations
attributes the penalty to the evaluation rather than to the system under test
says agreement exposes the cost as the gap between the ceiling and a perfect score

answers.answer: The caption rule removes a decision instead of advising on one, and it is checkable by someone who has never seen the page, which leaves no room for a house style. The same shape appears in the rule that every list item is an individual object instance labelled List-item, a definition that differs from PubLayNet and DocBank where list items are grouped into one List object. Rules at that precision do not fit on a page: the complete guideline runs over 100 pages, too long for the paper to describe. The authors claim a large improvement in consistency, not perfect consistency across the 40 staff.
accept: says an effective rule removes a decision and is checkable without seeing the page
gives a concrete rule such as one caption per picture or table, or list items as individual instances
notes the guideline runs to over 100 pages
says ambiguity is resolved once in the document rather than in each labeller's head
keeps the claim to improved consistency rather than perfect consistency

answers.answer: A bar the whole cohort clears has produced no information about the cohort, so it is evidence of nothing except that the exam was easy. DocLayNet's exam had 974 pages reference-annotated by one proficient core team member, and annotation staff annotated those same subsets blinded from the reference. Only staff who passed two exam levels with high annotation quality were admitted to production. Practice iterations ran over 12 weeks, after which 8 of the 40 initially allocated annotators did not pass the bar, and production was carried out by the remaining 32.
accept: says a bar everyone clears yields no information about the cohort
describes annotating pages blinded against a core team member's reference annotation
notes that admission required passing two exam levels
gives the attrition, 8 of 40 failing after 12 weeks, leaving 32 for production

answers.answer: Two labellers who can see each other converge, so the figure measures how readily the second deferred to the first rather than how far two independent readings of the guideline coincide. A ceiling built from conformity sits higher than the real one, so every model measured against it looks worse than it is. DocLayNet blocked this by design: annotation staff were not able to see each other's annotations, enforced specifically to avoid bias that could skew the inter-annotator agreement numbers.
accept: says the number measures conformity or deference rather than independent agreement
says the resulting ceiling sits higher than the true one
says models measured against an inflated ceiling look worse than they are
says DocLayNet prevented annotators from seeing each other's annotations, by design
